formNote: Add 을 after a consonant and 를 after a vowel, then 좋아해요. The thing you like takes the object marker, not 이/가.
examples: I like winter more than summer.
mistakes: Do not use 이/가 here. Say 김치를 좋아해요, not 김치가 좋아해요.

english: to go by N / toward N
formNote: Add 로 after a vowel or ㄹ, and 으로 after other consonants. It marks a means of transport or a direction.
examples: I go to work by subway.
Let us go by taxi, there is no time.
mistakes: For transport use 로/으로, not 에. Say 버스로 가요, not 버스에 가요.

english: to go in order to V
formNote: Add 러 to a vowel stem and 으러 to a consonant stem, then a movement verb like 가요 or 와요. It shows the purpose of going.
usage: I go to meet a friend.
I go to buy a book.
examples: I am going to eat lunch.
I go to the library to study.
Tomorrow I go to meet a friend.
mistakes: Use 러/으러 only with going or coming verbs like 가요, 와요.

formNote: Make the 아/어 form first: use 아 after ㅏ or ㅗ, otherwise 어, and 해 for 하다 verbs. Then add 보세요 to gently suggest trying.
examples: 저 카페에 가 보세요, 정말 좋아요.
Try that cafe, it is really nice.
mistakes: Pick the right vowel. Say 먹어 보세요, not 먹아 보세요.

formNote: Put the adjective before the noun. Add ㄴ after a vowel stem and 은 after a consonant stem. 있다/없다 adjectives use 는 instead.
examples: I live in a small house.
I want to eat delicious food.
mistakes: The adjective comes before the noun, not after it.

english: a noun that does the verb
formNote: Attach 는 to the plain verb stem to describe a noun doing that action now. ㄹ stems drop the ㄹ, so 살다 becomes 사는.
examples: 저기 책을 읽는 사람이 제 친구예요.
The person reading a book there is my friend.
I took the train going to Busan.
The place I live is Seoul.
mistakes: For present action use 는, not the past or future modifier.

english: it seems like N / looks like N
formNote: Put a noun before 같아요 to say something resembles it or seems to be it. No object marker is needed before 같아요.
examples: This painting looks like a photo.
mistakes: Do not add 을/를 before 같아요. Say 학생 같아요.

formNote: Attach 보다 to the thing being compared, then 더 plus the adjective. 더 means more and is often optional but natural.
examples: The subway is faster than the bus.
제 동생이 저보다 더 키가 커요.
My sibling is taller than me.
mistakes: 보다 attaches to the standard you compare against, not the subject.

formNote: Attach 기로 했어요 to a plain verb stem to report a decision you already made. The 했어요 part is fixed in the past.
examples: I decided to go to Korea next year.
I decided to exercise every day from today.
mistakes: Keep 했어요 in the past even for future plans.

formNote: Put a time-length noun before 동안 to show how long something lasts. No particle is needed between the noun and 동안.
examples: I waited for the bus for one hour.
During the vacation I went to Korea.
I studied Korean for three years.
mistakes: No particle before 동안. Say 한 시간 동안, not 한 시간에 동안.
